js_003: Which British evolutionary biologist wrote The Selfish Gene?
js_008: The Selfish Gene is a 1976 popular-science book by British evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins. It made the world see evolution through ‘the eyes of the gene’.
js_010: In which year did this book first appear?
js_015: The Selfish Gene first came out from Oxford University Press in 1976. A revised edition followed in 1989, the 30th-anniversary edition in 2006, and the 40th in 2016.
js_017: What does the book see as the fundamental unit of natural selection?
js_022: Dawkins saw the real unit that natural selection acts on as the gene — not the individual or the species. Genes compete to survive.
js_024: What did Dawkins call our bodies (individual organisms)?
js_028: Dawkins called the body a survival machine, built and steered by genes. The body is basically a ‘vehicle’ that carries genes around.
js_030: What word — coined and spread by Dawkins in this book — means a unit of cultural transmission?
js_034: A meme is a ‘cultural replicator’ — songs, catchphrases, fashions that copy from person to person. Dawkins coined it in Chapter 11 of this book, echoing the word ‘gene’.
js_036: What is the title actually calling ‘selfish’?
js_039: The ‘selfish’ in the title points to the gene, not to humans. It’s a metaphor: genes act as if they’re trying to make more copies of themselves — it doesn’t mean genes have minds.
js_041: What key term for the gene means ‘a thing that copies itself’?
js_045: Dawkins calls the gene a self-replicator. The history of life, he says, is the story of these replicators competing to survive by copying themselves exactly.
js_047: Where does Dawkins say the first self-replicator arose by chance?
js_051: In the sea before life began — the so-called primordial soup — a molecule that copied itself appeared by chance. The competition among these replicators is where evolution begins.
js_053: The body dies, but the gene lives on through copies. Which phrase best matches how Dawkins describes it?
js_055: Lives just one generation, then vanishes
js_058: Dawkins calls the gene ‘the immortal coil’. The body vanishes within a generation, but the gene can survive for millions of years through its copies.
js_060: To the question of whether humans are ruled by their selfish genes forever, what’s Dawkins’ answer?
js_061: Humans alone can rebel against the gene’s rule
js_062: Humans are just puppets of their genes too
js_064: Even civilization runs on the genes’ orders
js_065: Dawkins’ conclusion is surprisingly hopeful. Only humans who understand the logic of the selfish gene can defy its commands and choose to live altruistically.
js_072: EBS Class-e: Reading The Selfish Gene (KR)
js_073: Richard Dawkins (b. 1941) is an evolutionary biologist and former Oxford professor. The Selfish Gene made him world-famous; he went on to write The Blind Watchmaker, The God Delusion, and more.
js_074: After the 1976 first edition, Dawkins added two new chapters in the 1989 revised edition — ‘Nice Guys Finish First’ and ‘The Long Reach of the Gene’. That’s the version widely read today.
js_075: The core question is ‘what gets selected?’ Dawkins argued the unit of natural selection is the gene, not the individual or species. The individual is just a vessel the gene briefly inhabits.
js_076: A survival machine is the body genes build to protect and carry themselves. Our eyes, hands, brains, and behavior are all devices honed to help genes survive.
js_077: ‘Meme’ comes from a Greek word for ‘imitation’, shaped to sound like ‘gene’. Like songs, catchphrases, and technologies, it’s a cultural replicator that copies from brain to brain.
js_078: ‘Selfish’ is a metaphor aimed at the gene. It’s not that genes have desires — they just ‘appear to act’ in ways that favor leaving more copies of themselves.
js_079: A replicator is anything that copies itself. Dawkins rewrites the history of life as ‘the story of replicators competing to survive’.
js_080: The primordial soup is the chemical broth of the pre-life sea. In it, a self-copying molecule arose by chance, and whichever copied better survived — and evolution began.
js_081: The body disappears within a generation, but the gene carries on through copies. That’s why Dawkins calls the gene ‘the immortal coil’ — a thing that practically never dies.
js_082: Dawkins’ conclusion is hopeful. Humans who grasp the logic of the selfish gene can ‘choose’ to live altruistically, against the selfishness their genes push for.
js_095: ↻ This one will come back later
js_097: The real unit of natural selection is not the individual or the species — it’s the gene. A gene is a self-replicator competing to leave copies of itself.
js_099: Our body is a survival machine that genes build and steer — a vehicle that carries genes around.
js_100: Relatives share genes with you. Helping relatives means helping your own genes — so altruism toward family evolves.
js_102: Like the hawk–dove game, it’s a stable pattern of behavior that can’t be overturned even when a rival strategy invades.
js_104: If you’ll meet again, helping each other and paying it back benefits both sides’ genes. It’s the root of cooperation between strangers.
js_105: A cultural replicator — songs, catchphrases, fashions — that copies from brain to brain. Dawkins coined the word in this book.
js_106: Like a beaver’s dam, a gene’s effects reach beyond the body into the environment. A gene’s power isn’t trapped inside the body.
js_107: Humans who understand the selfish gene are the only beings that can defy its commands and live altruistically.
js_109: Why we exist — the birth of the replicator
js_110: To the question ‘why do we live?’, Dawkins looks for the answer through the eyes of the gene.
js_111: In the pre-life primordial soup, a molecule that copies itself — the replicator — first appears.
js_112: Replicators that copy more accurately, faster, and longer survive and multiply.
js_113: Today’s descendants of that replicator are exactly what we call genes.
js_115: The immortal coil & the survival machine
js_116: The body vanishes within a generation, but the gene leaps across millions of years through copies.
js_117: The gene builds and steers a body to carry it — the ‘survival machine’.
js_118: Brains, muscles, and behavior are all devices honed to help the gene survive.
js_119: The view that the body is the gene’s ‘vehicle’ is the heart of this book.
js_122: The hawk–dove game explains why aggression stops at a certain line (ESS).
js_123: Relatives share your genes, so helping a relative is helping your own genes.
js_124: Hamilton’s rule, rB > C — when benefit × relatedness beats the cost, altruism evolves.
js_125: Even a parent’s love for its child ultimately comes down to a gene’s-eye ‘calculation’.
js_127: Family planning & the war of generations and sexes
js_128: Animals don’t just breed as much as possible — they adjust their number of offspring to what they can raise.
js_129: Offspring want a bit more while parents want to share evenly — so weaning conflict arises.
js_130: The split between the large, costly egg and the small, cheap sperm sets the sexes’ strategies apart.
js_131: The female’s caution and the male’s competition — the game of push and pull starts here.
js_133: Cooperation by paying it back, and the meme
js_134: If you’ll meet again, reciprocal altruism — helping and paying back — evolves.
js_135: In Chapter 11, Dawkins first proposes the cultural replicator, the ‘meme’.
js_136: Like songs, catchphrases, fashions, and tech, memes also go through copying, mutation, and competition.
js_137: Memes spread far faster than genes, from just about anyone to anyone.
js_139: Nice guys finish first · The long reach of the gene
js_140: In the repeated prisoner’s dilemma, tit-for-tat — which ‘cooperates first’ — wins.
js_141: A ‘nice’ strategy that never defects first turns out to pay off best in the long run.
js_142: Like a beaver’s dam, a gene’s effects reach out into the world beyond the body (the extended phenotype).
js_143: Yet humans alone can understand the gene’s selfishness — and stand against it.
js_144: The worker bee that gives its life
js_145: A worker bee that stings dies, but it defends the hive. As an individual it’s suicide — but since the queen and sisters share its genes, from the ‘gene’s eye’ it pays off.
js_146: That an individual’s sacrifice can benefit its genes — this case shows at a glance why kin selection is so powerful.
js_147: The cuckoo that dumps its eggs in another’s nest
js_148: A cuckoo secretly lays its egg in another bird’s nest, and its chick shoves out the original eggs. The host bird, tricked into raising a stranger’s chick, is being manipulated by cuckoo genes.
js_149: One creature’s genes can even change another creature’s behavior — it makes you think about the ‘extended phenotype’ and the arms race between genes.
js_150: The vampire bat that shares its blood
js_151: A vampire bat regurgitates the blood it drank to share with a starving companion. This sharing holds up on a footing of paying it back — give today, get it back when you’re the hungry one.
js_152: Even without kinship, cooperation evolves as long as ‘paying it back’ works — the classic example of reciprocal altruism.
js_153: If my body is the gene’s ‘survival machine’, then what on earth is the ‘me’?
js_154: Genes made you — but it’s also you who read this book and now ‘know’ that. Think about how far that knowing can change you.
js_155: How can ‘altruistic’ behavior come out of a ‘selfish’ gene?
js_156: Think of kin selection, reciprocity, and paying it back. It’s worth chewing on the paradox that selfishness and cooperation actually spring from the same root.
js_157: If memes are ‘selfish’ just like genes, are the thoughts in my head really mine?
js_158: Some beliefs and trends may have stuck around not because they benefit you, but simply because they ‘spread well’. Ask yourself who your convictions really serve.
